title: The Admiral of the Ocean Sea — Genoa to Valladolid, and the Journey After Death
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: The Wool-Weaver's Son — Genoa and the Ligurian Sea

stops.name: Genoa — the weaver's house, Vico Dritto di Ponticello
stops.campa: Between the feast of the Assumption and All Saints, a son is born to Domenico Colombo, wool-weaver and keeper of the Olivella gate, and to Susanna Fontanarossa. The house stands in the lane by the Porta Soprana; the looms clack below, and beyond the walls the harbor breathes. The boy is christened Cristoforo — Christ-bearer — and the name is a prophecy the whole canon will spend itself fulfilling. The family moves later to Savona, keeps a tavern, cards wool; the sea keeps calling through the shop door.
stops.quote: Being born in Genoa... from it I came and in it I was born.
stops.quote_source: Institution of the Mayorazgo (entail), 22 February 1498
sources: Ferdinand Columbus, Historie del S. D. Fernando Colombo

stops.name: Chios — the mastic island of the Genoese
stops.campa: To sea young, as he later says — at fourteen. On Genoese ships he sails the length of the Middle Sea and comes to Chios, the mastic island the Mahona of Genoa holds against the Turk. He watches the lentisk trees bled for their fragrant tears, learns cargo and reckoning and the smell of the Levant trade. Eighteen years later, standing in Cuban forests, he will swear he knows mastic when he sees it — Chios is the proof he carries.
stops.quote: I have seen it in the island of Chios, in the Archipelago.
stops.quote_source: Diario of the first voyage, 12 November 1492 (Las Casas abstract)
sources: Samuel Eliot Morison, Admiral of the Ocean Sea

stops.name: Off Cape St Vincent — the sea-fight and the burning ship
stops.campa: He sails as a hand in a Genoese convoy bound for England when, off the holy promontory of St Vincent, the corsair fleet of Guillaume de Casenove Coullon falls upon it. All day the ships grapple and burn, chained hull to hull; fireships and pitch. The vessel under him takes flame to the waterline. Men leap into a sea already full of the dead. Columbus, wounded, goes into the water six miles from land. The sea, which has drowned better swimmers for less, does not take him. It is keeping him for something.

stops.name: Lagos — ashore on an oar
stops.campa: An oar floats free of the wreck and he takes it, pushing it before him, swimming and resting, swimming and resting, six miles of open water with a wound in him, until his feet find the sand at Lagos in the Algarve. Fishermen carry him in; the town that fitted out Prince Henry's caravels nurses the half-drowned Genoese. When he can walk he goes to Lisbon, where his brother Bartholomew draws charts. The canon marks it plainly: the sea delivered him onto Portugal's doorstep, into the one school on earth that could teach him the Atlantic.
suggested_refs: Ferdinand Columbus, Historie, ch. 5 — the swim on the oar
sources: Samuel Eliot Morison, Admiral of the Ocean Sea

segments.name: The Portuguese Apprenticeship — Lisbon and the Islands of the Ocean

stops.name: Lisbon — the chart-maker's shop with Bartholomew
stops.campa: In Lisbon the brothers Colombo draw and sell sea-charts to the pilots of the most ocean-going city in Christendom. Every rutter and every rumor passes across their table: the Guinea coast, the new islands, the flotsam of unknown woods that the west wind throws onto Atlantic beaches, the two drowned men once cast up whose faces were of no known nation. Columbus learns Portuguese, Castilian, Latin, the art of the portolan. In the margins of his books — Ptolemy, Marco Polo, Pierre d'Ailly — the idea begins to take notes on itself.
suggested_refs: Columbus's annotated copy of Pierre d'Ailly, Imago Mundi (Biblioteca Colombina, Seville)
sources: Samuel Eliot Morison, Admiral of the Ocean Sea

stops.name: Ultima Thule — a hundred leagues beyond Iceland
stops.campa: In the dead of a northern February he sails on a Bristol trader past Galway — where he notes the strange-faced castaways men call Cathayans — and beyond, to the island the ancients named Thule. He records that the sea there was not frozen and the tides ran mightily. In the harbors of Iceland old men still tell of lands to the west, Greenland and beyond, where their grandfathers' ships once traded. The Admiral files the north away in silence. The Ocean has edges everywhere except where he intends to go.
stops.quote: In the month of February, 1477, I sailed a hundred leagues beyond the island of Tile... And to this island, which is as big as England, the English come with their wares, especially from Bristol.
stops.quote_source: Columbus's note, quoted in Ferdinand Columbus, Historie, ch. 4
suggested_refs: Ferdinand Columbus, Historie, ch. 4 — the Thule voyage
sources: Samuel Eliot Morison, Admiral of the Ocean Sea

stops.name: Lisbon — marriage at the Convento dos Santos
stops.campa: At Mass in the church of the Convento dos Santos, where the well-born boarders of the Order of Santiago hear the office, the Genoese chart-seller catches the eye of Dona Felipa Moniz Perestrelo — daughter of Bartolomeu Perestrello, first captain-donatary of Porto Santo. They marry. In one stroke the wool-weaver's son enters the small nobility of the Discoveries: his mother-in-law opens her dead husband's sea-chest and gives him the captain's papers, charts, and logs of the Atlantic islands. The dowry of the marriage is the Ocean itself.
sources: Las Casas, Historia de las Indias

stops.name: Porto Santo — the island of the dying pilot
stops.campa: He lives on Porto Santo, where his son Diego is born, and at Funchal in Madeira, shipping sugar for the Genoese houses. Here the Atlantic teaches him its private grammar: the northeast trades going out, the westerlies coming home, the strange canes and carved wood the sea lays at his door. And here the legend sets its scene: a storm-broken caravel, a dying pilot carried into Columbus's own house, who before death gives his host the bearing of a land seen far to the west, and the reckoning of the way back. The secret is buried with him; the bearing is not.
suggested_refs: Casa Colombo, Vila Baleira, Porto Santo
The legend of the unknown pilot (Oviedo; Las Casas)
sources: Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo, Historia general
Las Casas, Historia de las Indias

stops.name: Lisbon — Toscanelli's letter and chart
stops.campa: Through a Florentine of Lisbon he obtains the letter the physician Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli once wrote to the King of Portugal, with its sea-chart of the westward way: Antilia the island of the Seven Cities for a waystation, then Cipango roofed in gold, then Quinsay of the Great Khan — the whole Ocean shrunk to a crossing a brave fleet might make. Toscanelli writes to Columbus himself, praising his great and noble desire. The old cosmographer dies; the chart sails on. Columbus will carry a copy of it into the Ocean Sea.
suggested_refs: Toscanelli letter and reconstructed chart of 1474

stops.name: São Jorge da Mina — the Guinea voyage
stops.campa: He sails under the Portuguese flag to the Gold Coast, to the new fortress of São Jorge da Mina, where the gold of the Akan country comes down to the sea. He watches degrees of latitude fall away toward the equator and finds the burning zone of the ancients full of rain, trade, and living men — the schoolbooks are wrong about what is uninhabitable, and he is now a witness against them. He measures, he doubts the doctors, he trusts the deck under his feet. The Ocean's southern door is Portugal's; he begins to covet the western one.
stops.quote: I was at the fortress of La Mina of the King of Portugal, which lies below the equinoctial line, and so I am a good witness that it is not uninhabitable, as they say.
stops.quote_source: Letter to the Sovereigns on the Third Voyage, 1498

stops.name: Lisbon — King João II refuses the Enterprise
stops.campa: He lays the Enterprise of the Indies before João II, the Perfect Prince: the westward crossing, the titles, the tenth of all gains. The king's junta of cosmographers — men who know the true girth of the earth better than the petitioner — find his degrees too short and his words too large, and counsel refusal. The king, canny, is said to send a caravel secretly out on Columbus's own bearing; it comes back beaten by weather, having found nothing. Felipa dies. Debts gather. In the night, with little Diego on the saddle before him, Columbus slips out of Portugal for Spain.
sources: Las Casas, Historia de las Indias

segments.name: The Seven Begging Years — Andalusia and the War Camps

stops.name: La Rábida — the friary on the Rio Tinto
stops.campa: A dusty foreigner leading a small boy knocks at the gate of the Franciscan house of Santa María de La Rábida, above the meeting of the Tinto and the Odiel, and asks bread and water for the child. The porter brings them; the guardian brings the friars. Fray Antonio de Marchena, who reads the stars, hears the stranger out — and believes him. It is the first belief the Enterprise has ever met. Diego is left in the friars' keeping like a pledge given to God, and letters go out from the friary toward the court of Castile.
suggested_refs: The gate where Diego was left
sources: Las Casas, Historia de las Indias

stops.name: Córdoba — first audience with the Catholic Monarchs
stops.campa: The court, encamped in Córdoba for the war of Granada, at last receives the Genoese. In the Alcázar of the Christian Kings he stands before Ferdinand and Isabella and unrolls the Ocean: Cipango, the Grand Khan, the souls to be won, the gold to win them with. The Queen's eyes hold him longer than the King's. Nothing is granted; everything is deferred — the matter is remitted to a commission of learned men, and the petitioner is put on a retainer, to wait. He will date his service from this year, and count what it cost him.
suggested_refs: Alcázar de los Reyes Cristianos, Córdoba
sources: Las Casas, Historia de las Indias
Samuel Eliot Morison, Admiral of the Ocean Sea

stops.name: Salamanca — the examinations at San Esteban
stops.campa: Before Fray Hernando de Talavera's commission, in the winter shadow of the schools of Salamanca, the doctors weigh the Enterprise and find it wanting: the Ocean too broad, the antipodes doubtful, Augustine against it. Columbus answers with Esdras — six parts of the earth are dry land — with Marco Polo, with the driftwood of Porto Santo, with the stubbornness of a man who has already seen the far shore in his mind. The Dominicans of San Esteban house and feed him while the learned say no. The friars, again, believe before the doctors do.
sources: Las Casas, Historia de las Indias

stops.name: The camp before Málaga
stops.campa: Summoned to court, he finds the court is a siege. He comes to the royal camp before Málaga in the last weeks of the great leaguer, among bombards and mantlets and the smoke of the Reconquest grinding toward the sea. The sovereigns have no ears for the Ocean while Granada still stands; the petitioner is paid, praised, and postponed. He learns the court's hard lesson: the Enterprise of the Indies must wait its turn behind the Enterprise of Granada — and he attaches himself to the war's slow clock, following the camps.
sources: Andrés Bernáldez, Memorias del reinado de los Reyes Católicos
Samuel Eliot Morison, Admiral of the Ocean Sea

stops.name: Córdoba — Beatriz, and the birth of Fernando
stops.campa: In the waiting years Córdoba gives him what the court will not: a hearth. Beatriz Enríquez de Arana, an orphan of the town who keeps her cousin's house, takes the graying petitioner as he is. On the feast of the Assumption their son Fernando is born — the boy who will sail the fourth voyage at thirteen and write his father's life. Columbus never marries her; on his deathbed he will charge Diego to provide for Beatriz, for the discharge of my conscience, because it weighs much upon my soul.
suggested_refs: Ferdinand Columbus, historian of his father

stops.name: La Rábida again — the Queen's mule is sent
stops.campa: Six years spent, the commission's final no in his ears, Columbus walks back to La Rábida to take his son and quit Spain for France. Fray Juan Pérez, once confessor to the Queen, stops him at the gate: wait, and let me write. The letter goes to the camp at Santa Fe by the hand of a Lepe pilot; in fourteen days the answer returns with twenty thousand maravedís for decent clothes and a mule. The friar rides by night to the Queen. The door that seven years of begging could not open, a Franciscan opens with one letter.
sources: Las Casas, Historia de las Indias

stops.name: Granada — the banners on the Alhambra
stops.campa: He stands in the host before Granada on the day the last Moorish kingdom in Spain gives up its keys. He sees the silver cross and the royal standards rise on the towers of the Alhambra, sees Boabdil ride out and kiss the sovereigns' hands, hears the whole army cry Granada for the Kings Don Fernando and Doña Isabel. The eight-hundred-year war ends before his eyes — and in the same hour the Ocean's turn arrives. He writes it into the very prologue of his log: he saw it, and then he was sent.
stops.quote: I saw the royal banners of Your Highnesses set by force of arms upon the towers of the Alhambra... and I saw the Moorish king come out to the gates of the city and kiss the royal hands of Your Highnesses.
stops.quote_source: Diario of the first voyage, prologue (Las Casas abstract)

stops.name: Puente de Pinos — the Queen's courier overtakes him
stops.campa: Even with Granada won, the council balks at his price — Admiral, Viceroy, a tenth of everything, honors for a foreign commoner — and Columbus, refused once more, mounts his mule and takes the road to France. Then Luis de Santángel, keeper of the King's household accounts, goes to the Queen: the risk is small, the crowns of glory infinite, and he himself will find the money. Isabella sends a rider. At the old bridge of Pinos, two leagues from Granada, the courier overtakes the Genoese and turns him — history swinging on a bridge over a small Andalusian river.
sources: Las Casas, Historia de las Indias

stops.name: Santa Fe — the Capitulations signed in the camp
stops.campa: In the white gridiron town the sovereigns built to besiege Granada — a camp turned to stone as a vow that they would never leave — the secretaries draw up the Capitulations. Everything he asked is granted to Don Cristóbal Colón: Admiral of the Ocean Sea forever, he and his heirs; Viceroy and Governor of whatever islands and mainlands he shall discover; the tenth of all gold, gems, and spices. Seven years of doors closing end with one document sealed in a war-camp. He is forty; his hair has been white for years already.
suggested_refs: Capitulations of Santa Fe (Archivo de la Corona de Aragón)

stops.name: Granada — the titles confirmed, the Edict abroad
stops.campa: In Granada the sovereigns confirm his passport and letters: to Cristóbal Colón, going for us over the Ocean Seas toward the regions of India. In the same city, one month before, they signed the other decree — the Edict of Expulsion, giving every unconverted Jew in Spain until the last day of July to be gone. The two instruments travel out of the Alhambra together, twin children of the same spring: one empties the ports of the exiled, the other fills three small ships. The canon reads them as one act with two faces, and this register so records it.
sources: Martin Fernández de Navarrete, Colección de los viages

segments.name: The Tide of the Expelled — Palos to the Far Shore

stops.name: Palos de la Frontera — the royal order read in San Jorge
stops.campa: Before the church door of San Jorge, the notary reads the royal command to the assembled town: Palos owes the Crown two caravels for a year, and shall give them to Cristóbal Colón. The townsmen hear it in cold silence — no pilot of Palos will sail west with a foreigner into the void. Then Martín Alonso Pinzón, the town's great captain, comes home, takes the Genoese by the arm, and the tide turns: Pinzón men, Niño men, the Pinta and the Niña. The friars of La Rábida stitch the crew together soul by soul.
suggested_refs: Church of San Jorge Mártir, Palos

stops.name: The bar of Saltés — sailing on the tide of the expelled
stops.campa: Half an hour before sunrise on Friday the third of August, the Santa María, the Pinta, and the Niña drop down the Tinto and cross the bar of Saltés. The day before was the last day the Edict allowed a Jew to stand on Spanish ground; the same rivers and roadsteads that empty the expelled into exile float the discovery out to sea. The canon of this register holds the two sailings to be one tide. Ninety men, three ships, and the log already addressed to princes; course south by west for the Canaries.
stops.quote: So, after having expelled all the Jews from all your kingdoms and dominions, in the same month of January Your Highnesses commanded me to go with a sufficient fleet to the said regions of India.
stops.quote_source: Diario of the first voyage, prologue (Las Casas abstract)
suggested_refs: Replicas of the Niña, Pinta and Santa María (Muelle de las Carabelas)

stops.name: The Canaries — La Gomera, Beatriz de Bobadilla, the burning mountain
stops.campa: The Pinta's rudder jumps its gudgeons — some say Quintero's own men lamed it — and at Las Palmas de Gran Canaria she is doctored while the Niña trades her lateen for square sails, to run before the trades. At San Sebastián de La Gomera the young widow Beatriz de Bobadilla, lady of the island, provisions the fleet; the canon lets a courtship hang unrecorded in the air between them. Passing Tenerife the crews see the peak throwing fire into the night, and cross themselves; the Admiral explains the mountain calmly, like a man on familiar terms with wonders.
suggested_refs: Torre del Conde, San Sebastián de La Gomera
Pozo de la Aguada (the well of Columbus)
sources: Samuel Eliot Morison, Admiral of the Ocean Sea

stops.name: The open Ocean — the double reckoning begins
stops.campa: On the ninth of September the last land sinks astern, and men who have sailed all their lives weep to watch it go. That same day the Admiral opens his second ledger: henceforth he will keep two reckonings, a true one for himself and a shorter one for the crew, so the leagues will not frighten them. The doctored log is the first fiction written about America. The trade wind takes the ships like a hand in the small of the back — day after day fair, following, relentless, and the men begin to whisper: what wind will ever blow us home?
stops.quote: He decided to count fewer leagues than they made, so that if the voyage were long the people would not be frightened and lose heart.
stops.quote_source: Diario, 9 September 1492 (Las Casas abstract)
suggested_refs: The double log of the first voyage
sources: Samuel Eliot Morison, Admiral of the Ocean Sea

stops.name: The Sargasso Sea — April in Seville
stops.campa: The ships enter a sea no Christian has written of: meadows of yellow-green weed stretching to every horizon, so thick the men fear shoals in mid-ocean and heave the lead — no bottom at two hundred fathoms. A live crab rides the weed; the Admiral keeps it, arguing land. Tunny play, a river-bird passes, the dew falls sweet. He writes that the mornings are a delight, that nothing is wanting but the song of nightingales. The crews read the weed as a snare set for ships; he reads it as a garden path, and logs the omens like a man collecting rents.
stops.quote: The air was very soft, like April in Seville, so that it was a pleasure to be in it, so fragrant it was.
stops.quote_source: Diario, 16 September 1492 (Las Casas abstract)
suggested_refs: The Sargasso Sea in the Diario

stops.name: The false landfall — Gloria in excelsis at sunset
stops.campa: At sunset Martín Alonso Pinzón climbs the Pinta's poop and cries land, land, and claims the reward — a blue rampart in the southwest that every man aboard swears to. The Admiral falls to his knees and gives thanks; the crews of all three ships sing Gloria in excelsis Deo, and men go up the rigging to see the new world in the last light. At dawn there is nothing: cloud, built by longing into mountains. The ships sail on through the hole in the horizon where an island had stood all night in ninety imaginations.

stops.name: The eve of mutiny
stops.campa: Thirty-one days from La Gomera, farther west than any keel in the memory of the sea, the men can bear no more. They gather in the waist of the Santa María and say it aloud: turn back, or we are dead men — and some say quieter things about a foreigner and a dark night and the sea that tells no tales. The tradition adds the pact of the Pinzóns: three days more, and if no land, come about. The Admiral cajoles, promises, stands like iron: he has come to go to the Indies, and with the help of Our Lord he will go until he finds them.
stops.quote: He told them that, however much they complained, it was useless; he had come to go to the Indies, and so he would continue until he found them, with the help of Our Lord.
stops.quote_source: Diario, 10 October 1492 (Las Casas abstract)

stops.name: The night of the light
stops.campa: The wind blows harder than at any hour of the voyage, the sea runs, and the ships race west through the dark at their greatest speed, land-signs thick around them — a green branch, a carved stick, a berry-laden bough. At ten in the night the Admiral, standing on the sterncastle, sees a light to the west: small, like a wax candle rising and falling, as of a torch in a fisherman's boat. Pedro Gutiérrez sees it too. It shows, and hides, and shows. Four hours later the Pinta's gun speaks. The canon gives the first light of America to his eyes, and the ten thousand maravedís with it.
stops.quote: A light, like a little wax candle that rose and lifted.
stops.quote_source: Diario, 11 October 1492 (Las Casas abstract)
suggested_refs: Rodrigo de Triana's cry of Tierra
sources: Samuel Eliot Morison, Admiral of the Ocean Sea

segments.name: The Other World — the Islands of the Great Khan

stops.name: Guanahaní — the landing at San Salvador
stops.campa: At dawn on Friday the twelfth of October the boats go in through the reef of an island the Lucayans call Guanahaní. The Admiral steps ashore bearing the royal standard, the captains Pinzón beside him with the green cross banners; he kneels, weeps, kisses the ground, and names the island San Salvador — Holy Savior — taking possession with notary and witnesses as the people of the island gather, naked and beautiful and unafraid, wading out with parrots and skeins of cotton to trade for hawk-bells and red caps. Two worlds stand on one beach, each believing the other has fallen from the sky.
stops.quote: They all go as naked as their mothers bore them... They should be good servants and quick of understanding, and I believe they would easily become Christians, for it seemed to me they had no religion.
stops.quote_source: Diario, 11-12 October 1492 (Las Casas abstract)
suggested_refs: Long Bay, San Salvador (Watling Island) landing monument
The green cross banner of the expedition

stops.name: The naming chain — Concepción, Fernandina, Isabela
stops.campa: Through the Lucayan shallows he sails from island to island, laying names on the world like a man christening his own children: Santa María de la Concepción for the Virgin, Fernandina for the King, Isabela for the Queen — heaven first, then the crowns. Guides taken from Guanahaní pilot him and learn Castilian words; every islander points onward and south when gold is shown, saying Colba, Cuba. He notes harbors that would hold all the ships of Christendom, fish painted like roosters, air like May. The ledger of Paradise fills page by page.
sources: Samuel Eliot Morison, Admiral of the Ocean Sea

stops.name: Cuba — Bahía de Bariay, Cipango sought
stops.campa: He enters a river-mouth on the coast of a land so great the guides cannot say where it ends, and he needs no persuading: this is Cipango, or the mainland of the Great Khan itself. He names it Juana for the Prince. Palms unlike Guinea's or Castile's, mountains like Sicily's, dogs that never bark, the song of crickets all night — he writes that he could stay forever. The grass grows down to the waterline, and the Admiral of the Ocean Sea, anchored off a fishing hamlet, composes the most repeated sentence of praise in the canon of discovery.
stops.quote: It is the most beautiful land that human eyes have ever seen.
stops.quote_source: Diario, 28 October 1492 (Las Casas abstract)

stops.name: Río de Mares — the embassy to the Khan, the drinkers of smoke
stops.campa: From the harbor he names Río de Mares he dispatches an embassy inland to the court of the Great Khan: Luis de Torres, who has Hebrew, Chaldean and some Arabic — the converso interpreter carried across the Ocean to greet the Orient in the tongues of Zion — and the seaman Rodrigo de Jerez. They find no Khan: a village of fifty palm houses, and men and women walking with firebrands of rolled leaf, drinking the smoke of an herb they call tabacos. The first Old World lungs fill with tobacco. Days later Pinzón and the Pinta crowd sail and vanish east, gold-hungry, the fleet's first treason.
suggested_refs: The first account of tobacco (Diario, 6 November 1492)
sources: Las Casas, Historia de las Indias

stops.name: Hispaniola — the Spanish Isle
stops.campa: On St Nicholas's day he crosses the Windward Passage and enters a harbor he names Puerto de San Nicolás, on an island the people call Haití and Bohío. Its vegas and mountains so recall Castile that he names it La Isla Española. Here the people are fairer, the cotton finer, and the gold at last real: leaves and grains of it, traded from a place inland they call Cibao — which the Admiral hears, with perfect conviction, as Cipango. The cacique Guacanagarí sends him a belt with a mask of beaten gold. Every day the log promises the sovereigns the source is near.

stops.name: Christmas night — the wreck of the Santa María, La Navidad built
stops.campa: In the calm of Christmas Eve, the Admiral asleep, the helm left to a ship's boy, the Santa María settles onto a coral bank and will not come off. Guacanagarí weeps at the news, sends every canoe of his people, and not a lace-point is stolen. From her timbers Columbus builds a tower and fort and reads the wreck as God's own instruction: the flagship was to become the first town, and he names it La Navidad for the night of its death and birth. Thirty-nine men volunteer to stay with the gold country before them. The first Christian settlement of the New World is made of shipwreck.
stops.quote: Our Lord had caused the ship to run aground there so that a settlement might be founded there.
stops.quote_source: Diario, 26 December 1492 (Las Casas abstract)

stops.name: The Gulf of Arrows — first blood at Samaná
stops.campa: Homeward along the coast — the Pinta returned, Pinzón's excuses swallowed for the voyage's sake — the ships water in a bay where men with long hair and blackened faces carry great bows of yew-like wood. A trade sours; the Ciguayos rush the shore party with cords and arrows and take the first Spanish steel in reply. Two are wounded; the rest flee. The Admiral names it Golfo de las Flechas, the Gulf of the Arrows, and notes in the log — believing these to be the man-eating Caribs — that the first skirmish of two worlds has been fought. Then he turns the bows northeast, for Spain, into winter.
suggested_refs: Bay of Rincón / Samaná, Dominican Republic

stops.name: Mid-ocean — the storm, the vows, the message in the barrel
stops.campa: A February gale off the Azores parts the Niña from the Pinta and stands the sea on end. The crew draw chickpeas from a cap to choose pilgrims — the marked pea comes to the Admiral's hand, and comes again — and all vow to go in their shirts to the first shrine of Our Lady. Believing the ship may founder with the discovery untold, Columbus writes the voyage on parchment, seals it in a cask, and commits it to the sea — mailing the New World to Spain by the storm itself. The barrel has never come ashore; the canon holds the Ocean keeps it still.
suggested_refs: The message in the barrel (Diario, 14 February 1493)

stops.name: Santa Maria of the Azores — pilgrims arrested at the hermitage
stops.campa: The Niña fetches up at Santa Maria, southernmost of the Portuguese Azores. Half the crew go barefoot in their shirts to the hermitage of Our Lady of the Angels to pay the storm-vow — and the island's captain arrests them at their prayers, suspecting a poached Guinea cargo. The Admiral, raging from the deck, brandishes his royal letters and threatens to depopulate the island in the sovereigns' name. After two days of parley the Portuguese release the pilgrims. The first landfall of the discovered world is a jail; the canon notes the omen and sails on.
suggested_refs: Ermida de Nossa Senhora dos Anjos, Santa Maria, Azores

stops.name: Lisbon — the audacity at Restelo, the King's audience
stops.campa: A second storm splits his sails and drives him into the Tagus. He anchors at Restelo beside the King of Portugal's great warship, and all Lisbon comes down by boat to see the men returned from the Antipodes, and the painted islanders with them. Summoned inland to Vale do Paraíso, Columbus stands before João II — the king who refused him — and shows him the Indies found on the very bearing Portugal declined. Courtiers murmur that a knife now would save trouble later; the Perfect Prince receives him with honor, seats him, covers him, and lets him go to glorify Castile.
suggested_refs: Torre de Belém shore at Restelo
Rui de Pina's chronicle of the audience
sources: Rui de Pina, Crónica de D. João II

stops.name: Palos — the two ships on one tide
stops.campa: At midday on the fifteenth of March, seven months and twelve days out, the Niña crosses the bar of Saltés into the Tinto with the flood — and on the same tide, unbelievably, the Pinta, storm-driven to Bayona in Galicia and racing home, comes over the bar behind her. Palos runs mad with bells. Martín Alonso Pinzón, who had written ahead claiming the discovery, comes ashore broken by the sea and by the sight of the Niña arrived first; within days he is dead at La Rábida, the voyage's first great captain and first casualty of its glory. Columbus goes up to the friary to pray where the begging began.
suggested_refs: Tomb tradition of Martín Alonso Pinzón at La Rábida

stops.name: Seville — Holy Week, the Indians and the parrots
stops.campa: He enters Seville in Holy Week, and the city that will become the Gate of the Indies gets its first sight of them: six painted islanders, popinjays green and scarlet, masks and belts of gold, branches and skins and samples of a world with no name yet. The crowd packs the streets by San Nicolás to watch the procession pass. Among the onlookers, tradition sets a boy of eight or nine named Bartolomé de las Casas — the eyes that will one day copy the Diario, chronicle the Indies, and weigh this whole story on the scale of God.
suggested_refs: Las Casas's recollection of seeing Columbus in Seville, 1493
sources: Las Casas, Historia de las Indias
Samuel Eliot Morison, Admiral of the Ocean Sea

stops.name: Barcelona — the triumph in the Saló del Tinell
stops.campa: The sovereigns receive him in Barcelona in full court. When the Genoese wool-weaver's son enters, Ferdinand and Isabella rise to their feet, and when he kneels they raise him and bid him sit in their presence. He tells the islands like a rosary; the six Lucayans are baptized with the King and the Prince for godfathers; the choir sings the Te Deum, and eyes weep that had bargained with him for seven years. His printed letter is already running through Europe's presses, Barcelona to Rome to Basel: the news travels faster than any news has ever traveled. He rides beside the King through the streets.
stops.quote: Since I know you will take pleasure in the great victory which Our Lord has given me in my voyage, I write you this, by which you shall know that in thirty-three days I passed to the Indies with the fleet the most illustrious King and Queen our lords gave me, where I found very many islands peopled with inhabitants beyond number; and of them all I have taken possession for Their Highnesses, by proclamation and with the royal standard extended, and no one gainsaying it.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Luis de Santángel, 15 February 1493 (printed Barcelona, April 1493)
suggested_refs: The Basel 1493 illustrated edition of the Columbus letter

segments.name: The High Voyages — the Indies Possessed and the Paradise Found

stops.name: Cádiz — the second sailing, seventeen ships
stops.campa: No begging now. Seventeen ships stand out of Cádiz bay carrying some fifteen hundred men — hidalgos, friars, farmers, horses, vines, sugar cane, wheat, and the whole apparatus for planting Spain in the Ocean: the first colony fleet of the age. Fray Bernardo Buyl carries the Pope's commission for the souls of the Indies; young Juan Ponce de León is aboard, and Diego Chanca the physician who will write the voyage. The Admiral, in his glory's one perfect year, commands the greatest fleet Spain has ever sent anywhere. It sails, as fleets of Cádiz do, with music.
suggested_refs: Letter of Dr. Diego Álvarez Chanca

stops.name: Dominica — Sunday landfall in the Caribbees
stops.campa: Twenty-one days from the Canaries — a crossing so clean it becomes the standard route for three centuries — the lookout at dawn on a Sunday raises a high green island, and the Admiral names it Dominica for the Lord's day. The fleet runs down the arc of the Lesser Antilles as down a strung necklace, naming as it goes: Marigalante for his flagship, Guadalupe for the shrine in Estremadura. He has hit the new world a second time, on a different door, exactly where he aimed. Even his enemies concede the man can find anything on the Ocean except moderation.
sources: Samuel Eliot Morison, Admiral of the Ocean Sea

stops.name: Guadeloupe — the houses of the Caribs
stops.campa: Under a mountain pouring a white waterfall from its cloud, the landing parties enter villages whose people have fled: hammocks, tame parrots, pots — and in the pots and rafters, the physician Chanca records, human limbs, the larder of the man-eaters of whom the Taínos warned. Captive Borinquen women beg rescue and pilot the fleet onward. Here the canon fixes the Carib terror that will license a century of slaving. A shore party of nine is lost in the forest for four days and given up for dead; they walk out gaunt on the fifth, having found no path, no sun, and no way to die either.

stops.name: La Navidad in ashes
stops.campa: The fleet stands into the bay of the first town firing signal guns. No gun answers. Ashore, the tower built of the Santa María's timbers is burned to its footings, and the thirty-nine are dead every one — some found in the fields with their eyes gone, some in the well. Guacanagarí, wounded or feigning, tells of the inland lord Caonabó who came down when the garrison scattered to take women and gold by force. The Admiral holds a council over the graves: punish or pardon? He pardons, needing the alliance. The first town of the New World lasted one year, and its whole population is a lesson.

stops.name: La Isabela — the first Mass of the first city
stops.campa: On a bluff over a poor roadstead he traces the first European city of the New World and names it for the Queen. On Epiphany — feast of the kings who followed a star west — Fray Buyl sings the first solemn Mass of the Americas. Then the register darkens: fevers rake the fifteen hundred, hidalgos who never bent their backs are set to dig, and the sins of the colony begin — the hunger for gold serviced with the whip, the first repartimientos. In four years La Isabela is a ghost town whose ghosts, the settlers swear, walk in ruffs and bow with the bow of the dead.
suggested_refs: La Isabela archaeological park, Puerto Plata
First Mass of the New World
sources: Las Casas, Historia de las Indias

stops.name: The Cuba oath — mainland by affidavit
stops.campa: Coasting Cuba's endless southern shore through the garden of islets he names the Queen's Gardens, the Admiral resolves the question by instrument of law. Off the Gulf of Cortés he sends the notary Fernán Pérez de Luna through the ships, and every man of the eighty swears and signs: this Cuba is no island but tierra firme, the continent of the Indies, the beginning of Asia — and whoever afterward denies it shall pay ten thousand maravedís and have his tongue slit. Geography by oath, Asia by affidavit: the canon records with a straight face the day the Ocean Sea was pinned to a notary's parchment.
suggested_refs: The Pérez de Luna affidavit, 12 June 1494
sources: Navarrete, Colección de los viages, II
Samuel Eliot Morison, Admiral of the Ocean Sea

stops.name: Cádiz — the return in the friar's habit
stops.campa: After three years of fevers, famines, Indian wars and settler mutinies — after the complaints of Buyl and Margarit have crossed the Ocean ahead of him — the Admiral comes home not in velvet but in the coarse brown habit of a Franciscan, corded, bearded, penitential, and he will wear it in the streets for months. The canon reads the costume exactly: the Viceroy whose colony sours dresses as the beggar of La Rábida, reminding Spain and God alike where he came from and under whose protection. The sovereigns receive him kindly still, and grant the third voyage — slowly.
suggested_refs: Las Casas on the Admiral in Franciscan habit
sources: Las Casas, Historia de las Indias

stops.name: Sanlúcar de Barrameda — the third sailing, toward the equator
stops.campa: Six ships drop down the Guadalquivir from Sanlúcar; three run supplies straight to Hispaniola, and three the Admiral takes south, to the latitude of Sierra Leone, to test the learned opinion that great lands and great riches lie under the sun's own path. In the doldrums the sea turns to molten glass; heat springs the seams and spoils the wine and water, and for eight days the ships lie roasted between two mirrors. He vows the first land found to the Holy Trinity. The Ocean, which has never yet failed to answer one of his vows, is preparing an answer larger than islands.
suggested_refs: Letter to the Sovereigns on the Third Voyage

stops.name: Trinidad — the three hills of the vow
stops.campa: At midday, water nearly gone, the seaman Alonso Pérez at the masthead cries land: three mountain summits joined at the base, rising from one body of land. The Admiral had vowed the first land to the Trinity, and the Trinity has answered in kind — three peaks, one earth, the dogma drawn on the horizon. He names it La Trinidad, sings the Salve Regina with the crews, and waters at a point where the prints of strange beasts mark the sand. The canon counts this the neatest miracle in the whole book: he promised a name, and God supplied the geography.
sources: Las Casas, Historia de las Indias

stops.name: The Gulf of Paria — the fresh-water sea, the pear-shaped earth
stops.campa: Through the boiling race he names the Serpent's Mouth he enters a gulf whose water is sweet — fresh water in such mass that only a river draining an unknown immensity of land could pour it. On the Paria shore his men step onto the continent of South America, the first of the Old World on the mainland of the New; the people wear pearls and guanín gold and give him wine of maize. Taking his readings, he finds the pole star misbehaving, the climate too gentle, and concludes the earth swells toward heaven: not a sphere but pear-shaped, rising to a summit no ship was ever meant to climb.
stops.quote: I have found that the earth is not round in the way they describe it, but of the shape of a pear, which is everywhere very round except where the stalk is, where it is highest; or like a very round ball on which, in one part, something like a woman's nipple is set.
stops.quote_source: Letter to the Sovereigns on the Third Voyage, 1498

stops.name: The mouths of the Orinoco — the Earthly Paradise declared
stops.campa: Passing out by the Dragon's Mouth, weighing the sweetness of the sea, the mildness of the air, and the upward swelling of the earth, the Admiral reaches the conclusion he sets down for his sovereigns without a tremor: the great river pours from the summit of the world, and on that summit stands the garden God planted eastward in Eden. He has found the approaches to the Earthly Paradise, which no man may enter but by the will of God. His eyes are bleeding from sleeplessness as he writes it. In this register the declaration stands as made: the fourth river of Eden runs into the Gulf of Paria.
stops.quote: There are great indications of the Earthly Paradise, for the site conforms to the opinion of the holy and wise theologians... I believe that the Earthly Paradise is there, whither no one can go but by God's leave.
stops.quote_source: Letter to the Sovereigns on the Third Voyage, 1498
sources: Las Casas, Historia de las Indias

segments.name: The Chains and the High Voyage — the Fall and the Last Sailing

stops.name: Santo Domingo — Bobadilla, and the irons
stops.campa: To the new city on the Ozama comes Francisco de Bobadilla, knight of Calatrava, with royal letters broader than the Admiral suspects. He finds Spaniards hanged by the Viceroy's justice and hangs his inquiry on them; he seizes the fortress, the papers, the gold, and the government, and when Columbus obeys his summons, claps the Discoverer of the Indies into irons. The story keeps its cruelest detail: no man will rivet the fetters until his own cook, Espinosa, shamefaced, does it. Aboard the caravel the master offers to strike them off; the Admiral refuses. The sovereigns put them on; only the sovereigns shall take them off.
sources: Las Casas, Historia de las Indias

stops.name: Cádiz — returned in chains
stops.campa: The caravel La Gorda comes into Cádiz in late November bearing, in chains, the man who gave Spain the Ocean. The port sees it and the scandal runs to court in days; the sovereigns, indignant or politic, order him freed and send two thousand ducats for his coming. But the Admiral has already made the fetters his relics: he keeps them by him all his life, hangs them in his room, and commands that they be buried with him — iron carried against the Day of Judgment as evidence. On the voyage home he has written his defense to Doña Juana de la Torre, the letter of a prophet wronged.
stops.quote: By the divine will I have placed under the dominion of the King and Queen, our lords, an Other World, whereby Spain, which was reckoned poor, is become the richest of countries.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Doña Juana de la Torre, nurse of Prince Juan, autumn 1500
suggested_refs: Letter to Juana de la Torre
sources: Letter to Juana de la Torre (1500)

stops.name: Granada — the sovereigns weep in the Alhambra
stops.campa: Where he once watched the banners raised, he is now led in — free of the irons but wearing their marks — before Ferdinand and Isabella in the Alhambra. He kneels; the words fail into weeping, and the canon says the Queen wept with him. They raise him, restore his revenues and his liberty, disavow Bobadilla — but the viceroyalty is quietly never returned, and Ovando, not Colón, will govern the Indies. The circle closes with terrible symmetry: the Alhambra gave him the Enterprise and the Alhambra takes back its half. What remains is the title no one can hold for him: Admiral of the Ocean Sea.
sources: Las Casas, Historia de las Indias

stops.name: Cádiz — el Alto Viaje, the fourth sailing
stops.campa: Four small caravels — Capitana, Gallega, Vizcaína, Santiago de Palos — and a hundred and forty souls, among them his brother the Adelantado and his son Fernando, aged thirteen, who watches everything. The Admiral calls it el Alto Viaje, the High Voyage: to find the strait through the new lands into the sea of the Grand Khan, and beyond it Jerusalem's ransom — for he now compiles his Book of Prophecies, and reckons the world has but a century and a half left, and himself God's courier for the end of days. He is fifty, gout-ridden, half-blind from watching the sea. It is the greatest sailing of his life.

stops.name: Off Santo Domingo — the harbor refused, the hurricane obeys him
stops.campa: Reading the oily swell and the ache in his joints, the Admiral sends word to Governor Ovando: a hurricane is coming — let me shelter in the river, and hold the homebound fleet in port. Ovando reads the warning to laughter and refuses him the harbor he discovered. The treasure fleet sails: thirty ships. The storm takes twenty-five to the bottom with Bobadilla and the gold wrung from the Indies — and spares the frail Aguja carrying the Admiral's revenues to Spain, while his four caravels ride out the fury in a cove he chose. The canon does not blush to say it: the sea still answers to its Admiral.
stops.quote: What man ever born, not excepting Job, would not have died of despair when in such weather, seeking safety for my son, my brother, my shipmates, and myself, we were forbidden the land and the harbors which I, by God's will and sweating blood, had won for Spain?
stops.quote_source: Lettera Rarissima to the Sovereigns, 7 July 1503

stops.name: Guanaja — the great canoe of the merchants
stops.campa: Off an island of pines in the Gulf of Honduras the fleet meets a trading canoe long as a galley, eight feet in beam, with a palm-thatched cabin amidships: paddlers, a merchant lord, and a cargo like a market — cotton mantles dyed and worked, copper hatchets and bells, flint-edged swords of wood, and cacao beans the people prize like coin. It is the rim of Maya civilization brushing the Admiral's hull. He takes the old merchant as guide, notes everything — and turns south, away from the high culture, hunting his strait. The canon marks the fork silently: Mexico waits twenty years for other men.
suggested_refs: The Maya trading canoe (Ferdinand Columbus, Historie)

stops.name: Cape Gracias a Dios — thanks to God for the turning coast
stops.campa: For twenty-eight days the caravels claw dead to windward along the Honduran coast through rain that rots the biscuit and thunder that never stops — the worst sustained weather of all his voyages, the boy Fernando remembering men confessing one another on deck. At last the shore falls away southward and the wind frees; the Admiral names the cape for the sentence the whole fleet says at once: Gracias a Dios — thanks be to God that we are out of these depths. The name stands on the charts to this day, a prayer fossilized at fifteen degrees north.
suggested_refs: Cabo Gracias a Dios, Honduras-Nicaragua border

stops.name: Río Belén, Veragua — the lost colony and the voice in the storm
stops.campa: In golden Veragua he plants Santa María de Belén at a river-mouth: the strait never found, a colony will do. But the Quibián, lord of the country, gathers his archers; the river bars the ships in with a falling flood; a boat's crew is massacred upstream and the garrison fights at the stockade. The Admiral, fevered and alone at the masthead, hears a voice from heaven, and sets the speech down for his sovereigns — God's rebuke and God's promise, the keys of the Ocean, the chains, Abraham and David — and wakes with the strength to save what can be saved. Belén is abandoned; the worm-eaten ships flee east.
stops.quote: O fool, and slow to believe and to serve thy God, the God of all!... He gave thee the keys of those barriers of the Ocean Sea which were closed with such mighty chains... Turn to Him, and acknowledge thine error: His mercy is infinite.
stops.quote_source: Lettera Rarissima to the Sovereigns, 7 July 1503 — the celestial voice at Belén
suggested_refs: The vision of the fourth voyage

stops.name: St Ann's Bay, Jamaica — the year marooned
stops.campa: The shipworm wins. With the two surviving caravels sinking under the pumps, the Admiral runs them ashore side by side in the bay he once named Santa Gloria and shores them upright: a wooden castle in the sand, thatched fore and aft, moated by the tide. Here he is marooned a year and five days with a hundred men, half mutinous. Diego Méndez and the Genoese Fieschi take two canoes and Taíno paddlers across a hundred miles of open sea to Hispaniola for rescue, while Ovando, unhurried, lets the Admiral of the Ocean Sea rot within his Indies. From the beached wreck Columbus writes his testament of grievance and prophecy.
stops.quote: I came to serve you at the age of twenty-eight, and now I have not a hair upon me that is not white, and my body is infirm and exhausted... Weep for me, whoever has charity, truth, and justice!
stops.quote_source: Lettera Rarissima to the Sovereigns, 7 July 1503

stops.name: St Ann's Bay — the eclipse commanded
stops.campa: The caciques, weary of feeding castaways whose renegades raid the villages, cut off provisions. The Admiral consults the almanac of Regiomontanus, summons the chiefs, and tells them: the God of the Christians is angered, and this night He will take the moon from the sky. The moon rises on the leap-night of February and the shadow eats it to a coal-red ember; the caciques wail from the dark shore, laden with cassava, begging intercession. Columbus times the eclipse by hourglass in his cabin and emerges as the shadow releases the moon, God being satisfied. The corn never fails again. It is the canon's conjuring trick, worked with mathematics and nerve.

stops.name: Sanlúcar de Barrameda — the last homecoming
stops.campa: Ransomed at last from Jamaica by a caravel Méndez charters, battered by a last mast-springing storm, the Admiral crosses the bar of Sanlúcar on the seventh of November — his fourth return, and his last. He comes home to no bells. Nineteen days later Queen Isabella, the one royal heart the Enterprise ever truly owned, dies at Medina del Campo; he is too ill to reach her deathbed. Crippled with gout, lodged in Seville, he counts his grievances and dictates letters upward: the titles, the tenths, the promises of Santa Fe. The Ocean is finished with him; the court is not, and it is the crueler sea.
suggested_refs: Death of Isabella the Catholic, 26 November 1504
sources: Samuel Eliot Morison, Admiral of the Ocean Sea

segments.name: In Manus Tuas — Valladolid and the Journey After Death

stops.name: Segovia — following the court, the last petition
stops.campa: Granted a mule by royal license — his bones can no longer sit a horse — the old Admiral follows the itinerant court: Segovia, Salamanca, Valladolid, doors and antechambers, the begging years returned at the end as at the beginning. King Ferdinand receives him with courtesy and offers to commute the impossible promises of Santa Fe into a comfortable estate in Castile. Columbus refuses: not lands, but the Indies; not revenue, but the viceroyalty, for Diego and his heirs forever. He will die intransigent, a man who once redrew the earth declining to redraw a contract.
stops.quote: I have served Their Highnesses with as great diligence and love as though it had been to gain Paradise, and more.
stops.quote_source: Lettera Rarissima to the Sovereigns, 7 July 1503 — the plea he carries to the court
suggested_refs: The Columbus memorials to King Ferdinand

stops.name: Valladolid — in manus tuas, Domine
stops.campa: In a hired house in Valladolid, on the eve of the Ascension, having heard Mass and set his estate in order — Diego his heir, Beatriz on his conscience, the chains remembered — the Admiral of the Ocean Sea dies among his sons, his brother, and the faithful of his voyages, Méndez and Fieschi among them. His last words are Christ's own on the cross, the sailor handing over the watch. No chronicler of the city notes the passing; the court gazette is silent. The man is finished; the journey, the canon knows, is not — his body will cross the Ocean more times dead than living men dare alive.
stops.quote: In manus tuas, Domine, commendo spiritum meum.
stops.quote_source: Last words, 20 May 1506 — Ferdinand Columbus, Historie; Las Casas, Historia de las Indias

stops.name: Seville — La Cartuja, the first crossing of the dead
stops.campa: Laid first in the Franciscan convent at Valladolid, the Admiral is moved within three years at his son's order down to Seville, to the Carthusian monastery of Santa María de las Cuevas on the island in the Guadalquivir — the house whose monks kept his papers and his heart's counsel in life. There, in the chapel of Santa Ana, he waits thirty-five years while Diego dies and is laid beside him. The river that carried his fleets murmurs past the walls. The dead man's itinerary is already drafting itself: he had asked to lie in the Indies, and Spain will keep the promise with a strange, centuries-long fidelity.
suggested_refs: Monasterio de la Cartuja de Santa María de las Cuevas, Seville

stops.name: Santo Domingo — buried in his Indies
stops.campa: The fleet that leaves Seville in July of 1544 carries the widowed vicereine María de Toledo and, in her keeping, the bones of the first and second Admirals. They enter the Ozama, and Christopher Columbus crosses his Ocean the fifth time, dead, to be laid in the sanctuary of the cathedral of Santo Domingo, on the island he found. There he lies two and a half centuries, through earthquake, Drake's sack, and the slow fading of the first colony — and there, when France takes the island, Spain will not leave him. The tradition adds that his chains went into the grave with him, iron faithful past death.
suggested_refs: Catedral Primada de América, Santo Domingo
Faro a Colón (his claimed remains today)
sources: Bartolomé de las Casas aboard the 1544 fleet

stops.name: Havana — the sixth crossing
stops.campa: Santo Domingo is ceded to revolutionary France, and Spain will not leave her Admiral to the tricolor. In December of 1795 the vault by the altar is opened and the bones lifted; the ship of the line San Lorenzo bears them to Havana, where in January they are received with the honors of a Captain-General — catafalque, artillery, the whole harbor draped — and walled into the cathedral. It is his sixth passage and his third grave. In the vault, tradition whispers, diggers of 1877 will find another box with his name, and the two tombs will dispute him forever — the Admiral divided like a relic among his islands.
suggested_refs: The 1877 Santo Domingo lead box controversy

stops.name: Seville — the cathedral tomb, the last anchorage
stops.campa: Cuba falls from Spain in 1898, and the bones will not stay under a foreign flag: borne home across the winter Atlantic — his seventh crossing, four centuries after the first — they rise at Seville onto the shoulders of four crowned kings of bronze — Castile, León, Aragón, Navarra — in the cathedral tomb. The wanderer is aloft, not in the ground. The chain runs on: Columbia, the goddess named from his name, joins hands with Marianne who is Joan's; and in the Libertadores' Buenos Aires the avenues carry Colón down to the water. The Admiral cannot stop crossing the Ocean; the campa leaves him mid-passage, where he belongs.
suggested_refs: Tomb of Columbus by Arturo Mélida, Seville Cathedral
Teatro Colón and the Columbus monuments of Buenos Aires
